title: Autoregressive Models Rival Diffusion Models at ANY-ORDER Generation
claim: A two-stream attention design with distinct causal masks lets one model predict arbitrary token groups in arbitrary order.
layout: Bottom-to-top flow, two side-by-side mask panels, dashed divider, loss on top
description: An architecture diagram that reads bottom to top. At bottom left, the sentence 'The answer is 14 inches long' is embedded into hidden states H_q(1..6). Tokens are color-coded by group: teal for G1, purple for G3, orange for G2. At bottom right, a separate gray row of query-stream states appears. Arrows labeled Q,K,V and K,V, Q feed a large rounded box marked ×L. Inside it, two 6×6 attention-mask grids sit side by side, split by a dashed line. The left grid is the Content Stream and the right grid is the Query Stream. Blue cells mark allowed attention and white cells mark masked positions. Colored outlines highlight each group's block. At top, the final query-stream outputs H_q^L connect to the target tokens through a double-headed arrow labeled CE Loss.
caption: Architecture of the A3 model. Blue entries in the attention mask denote $0$, and white entries denote $-\infty$. The model employs a two-stream attention module with distinct causal masks. The content stream encodes contextual information and attends to tokens within its own group as well as all preceding groups. The query stream encodes positional conditions and attends only to tokens in preceding groups. The final cross-entropy loss is computed between the input context and the query stream’s output. For illustration, we provide an example grouping with $G_1=\{1,2,3\}, G_2=\{5,6\}, G_3=\{4\}$, showing how the forward process and causal masks are applied.
abstract: Diffusion language models enable any-order generation and bidirectional conditioning, offering appealing flexibility for tasks such as infilling, rewriting, and self-correction. However, their formulation-predicting one part of a sequence from another within a single-step dependency-limits modeling depth and often yields lower sample quality and stability than autoregressive (AR) models. To address this, we revisit autoregressive modeling as a foundation and reformulate diffusion-style training into a structured multi-group prediction process. We propose Any-order Any-subset Autoregressive modeling (A3), a generalized framework that extends the standard AR factorization to arbitrary token groups and generation orders. A3 preserves the probabilistic rigor and multi-layer dependency modeling of AR while inheriting diffusion models' flexibility for parallel and bidirectional generation. We implement A3 through a two-stream attention architecture and a progressive adaptation strategy that transitions pretrained AR models toward any-order prediction. Experiments on question answering, commonsense reasoning, and story infilling demonstrate that A3 outperforms diffusion-based models while maintaining flexible decoding. This work offers a unified approach for a flexible, efficient, and novel language modeling paradigm.
